title: Müller & Wrede, "Political Incentives in Local Tax Setting: Evidence from the German Property Tax Reform", CESifo Working Paper 13067 (October 2026)
what_was_fetched: Full text (54 pp.) of the open CESifo PDF https://www.ifo.de/DocDL/cesifo1_wp13067.pdf (1,078.84 kB), read through the r.jina.ai plain reader proxy, plus the ifo.de/CESifo landing page (abstract, citation, JEL codes). A direct request for the binary PDF (browser user-agent) returned HTTP 406 from ifo.de, so no PDF was saved; the text was obtained from the open PDF via the reader proxy. Saved: item1-muller-wrede-cesifo-wp13067-fulltext.txt, item1-ifo-landing-page.txt. Also read the current text of places/germany.md, research/loffler-siegloch-german-pass-through.md, research/kolbe-berlin-land-value-appraisal.md, research/buettner-german-land-tax-capitalization.md, objections/homevoters-will-block-lvt.md.
verdict: ENRICH places/germany.md (one paragraph in the Baden-Württemberg section plus a Sources row; the paper's only BW content is a control-group role and one footnote). Secondary ENRICH objections/homevoters-will-block-lvt.md (one or two sentences). No standalone research/ page recommended: the paper is not about land-only taxation or capitalization, and Baden-Württemberg is a comparison state, not an estimated one. A short research/ stub is defensible only if the queue wants a node for the 2025 Grundsteuer reform's political economy.
claim_grade: B (B-type empirical claim: staggered triple-difference on administrative data; unrefereed CESifo working paper). Source tier per EDITORIAL 4c: Tier 1 (CESifo Working Paper series; academic authors at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg, Wrede a CESifo Research Network Fellow). Not peer-reviewed; must be labelled a working paper. The tenant-incidence premise is NOT estimated here (borrowed from Löffler & Siegloch 2024), so any incidence statement stays graded on that paper, not this one.

content_summary.identification: Section 6.1, Eq. (5)-(7), pp. 17-21. Staggered difference-in-differences, then the preferred triple-difference (treated-state x owner-friendly council x post-announcement) with municipality FEs and state-by-year FEs (Eq. 7, the baseline). Event study uses the Borusyak-Jaravel-Spiess (2024) imputation estimator (Fig. 4, p. 22): pre-trend coefficients near zero, joint test p = 0.335, effect becomes significant (1% level) two years after announcement. Treatment = state adopted the federal model (Bundesmodell), whose standardized net rents per m2 (Annex 39 to s.254 Bewertungsgesetz) are higher for 'rental properties' than for single-/two-family homes: NRW, Rhineland-Palatinate, Saarland (Table A6, p. 44). Control = Baden-Württemberg, Bavaria, Hesse, Lower Saxony (opted out; their models 'do not explicitly distinguish' housing types, Section 3 p. 8). 'Post' starts the year after each state's model announcement (2020 or 2021; announcements in H2 coded to the next year because s.25 Grundsteuergesetz limits multiplier rises to H1). Political split: municipalities where homeowner-oriented parties (CDU/CSU, FDP, AfD, Freie Wähler; local Wählergruppen by default) or tenant-oriented parties (SPD, Linke, Grüne) won >50% of the vote throughout; small parties classified by an AI-based procedure (Table A4, p. 42). Placebo 2018/2019 shifts: 0.779 (s.e. 3.137) and 3.231 (3.224), Table A13 p. 50.
content_summary.headline_15pp_exact_wording: Abstract: "over an average post-announcement period of 3.6 years, municipal tax multipliers increased by 15 percentage points more when two conditions were met: municipalities were governed by homeowner-friendly parties and were located in states where tenants will face a higher tax base per square meter." The 3.6-year figure appears only in the abstract; the body never derives it (announcements 2020-21, sample ends 2024).
content_summary.headline_table: Table 2 (p. 20), column (2): triple interaction T x P x post = 15.017 (s.e. 4.674), p = 0.001, with state-by-year FEs; N = 30,032 municipality-years, 3,754 municipalities (clusters). Authors: 'a more conservative specification ... We adopt [it] as our baseline'; equals about 3.85% of the 2019 mean multiplier of 389.64. Column (1), municipality + year FEs only: 28.049 (4.647), about 7.20%. 'Percentage points' means points of the Hebesatz (e.g. 400% to 415%), not points of tax-rate share. Table 1 simple DiD (owner-friendly councils only): 31.248 (1.604); tenant-friendly councils 2.482 (5.103) n.s. Robustness (Tables A11-A14, pp. 48-51): major parties only 11.011 (5.113)**, excluding AfD 9.695 (5.240)*, excluding NRW 14.737***, excluding RLP 17.952***, NRW vs Hesse only 28.250 (11.202)**; state-level bootstrap SE (7 states) 8.316 with p = 0.071, i.e. significant only at 10% (Table A12 col. 4, text p. 30).
content_summary.heterogeneity: Table 3 (p. 23): above-median property-tax revenue share 16.841*** vs below 8.887 n.s.; above-median per-capita debt 22.612*** vs 5.756 n.s. Table 4 (p. 24): population growing 17.313*** vs declining 13.283*; >10,000 inhabitants 21.443*** vs <=10,000 10.133*. Table 5 (p. 26): replacing party orientation with municipal homeownership share gives a null (triple interaction near zero), so the mechanism is party orientation not electorate composition; authors call this 'suggestive rather than definitive' because ownership shares barely vary (60-80%). Table 6 (p. 28): business-tax multiplier +3.031** but ~0 once property-tax multiplier is controlled.
content_summary.descriptives: Data: property- and business-tax multipliers 2017-2024 from the Federal/State Statistical Offices (table 71231-01-03-5); local election results from state statistical offices on request; Census 2022; standardized net rents from BewG Annex 39. Sample: 7 West German non-city states (Schleswig-Holstein dropped for data; Bremen and Hamburg dropped because city-state governments chose their own model, making the reform endogenous). Mean multiplier, baseline sample, Table A3 (p. 41): 382.4 (2017), 389.6 (2019), 402.7 (2022), 418.7 (2023), 429.6 (2024). Owner-friendly municipalities in treated states: 430.9 (2017) to 521.7 (2024). Share of municipalities leaving the multiplier unchanged: 84.94% in the pre-announcement 3 years vs 56.69% in 2022-24; 22.74% raised it by 61-100 points (Fig. 1b, p. 13-14).
content_summary.valuation_models_by_state: Higher per-m2 base for rentals arises ONLY under the federal model (Bundesmodell), not under any state model. Federal-model states in sample: NRW (rentals highest in ~80% of the 15 size/age cells; 3 exceptions), Rhineland-Palatinate (all cells but one tie), Saarland (all cells). Example, Table A1 (p. 39), RLP, pre-1948, <60 m2: 7.12 EUR/m2/month single-family, 7.30 two-family, 8.33 rental. The federal model also applies rental values to owner-occupied apartments. Schleswig-Holstein and Bremen also use the federal model but are excluded; Hamburg has its own model and is excluded. Opt-out (alternative-model) states in sample: BW, Bavaria, Hesse, Lower Saxony. Footnote 10 (p. 9): these use 'building and living space, location quality, or land values'; area-based models 'implicitly tax building density at a lower rate'; 'Any implicit differences in the tax base per square meter tend to favor tenants rather than homeowners.' The paper does not individually describe the Bavarian Flächenmodell, the Hesse or Lower Saxony models, so the Bavaria/Hesse/Lower Saxony detail cannot be sourced from it.
content_summary.baden_wuerttemberg_and_land_value: Only two passages. (i) Footnote 10, p. 9: "Baden-Württemberg's land-value property tax system structurally favors multi-family housing over single- and two-family homes, as the tax base depends solely on land area and land values, irrespective of floor space index or structural density." This is the authors' characterization; no source or computation is given. (ii) Section 2 (p. 6): Murphy and Seegert (2026, Journal of Public Economics 261, 105735) is 'of direct relevance to the German tax reform - most notably for Baden-Württemberg - that opted for a land-value-based model under the reform's opening clause.' BW is in the control group and its own post-reform effects are not estimated. (The wiki already carries research/murphy-seegert-implicit-land-taxes.)
content_summary.incidence: Not estimated. Section 3 (p. 9) states landlords may pass the tax to tenants (s.556 BGB; s.2 Betriebskostenverordnung) and cites Löffler & Siegloch (2024, ECONtribute DP 331) for 'a high pass-through of the property tax onto tenants'. The theory section (Section 4, pp. 10-12) models renters as perceiving only a fraction gamma of the tax on rental housing as a burden, with the maintained condition gamma(1+delta) < 1; the key prediction (Eq. 3) is a negative interaction between renter welfare weight and the renter tax-burden parameter delta. The relevant prediction is about politicians' PERCEIVED incidence.

proposed_text_for_germany_md: Impersonal, Sources-only grade/access labels. Suggested sentence block (after the anchor): "A 2026 CESifo working paper by Ramona Müller and Matthias Wrede (Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg) uses the states' valuation-model choices as a natural experiment. Under the federal model, standardized net rents per square metre are higher for rental properties than for owner-occupied houses (in Rhineland-Palatinate, for pre-1948 units under 60 m², 8.33 euros against 7.12 and 7.30), while the alternative models of Baden-Württemberg, Bavaria, Hesse and Lower Saxony do not distinguish by housing type. Across 3,754 West German municipalities in 2017-2024, municipalities governed by homeowner-oriented parties in federal-model states raised their property-tax multipliers (Hebesätze) by about 15 points more than comparable municipalities in the alternative-model states, net of the corresponding gap among tenant-oriented councils (a triple-difference estimate, about 3.9% of the 2019 average multiplier).[n] Baden-Württemberg belongs to the comparison group, so the study does not measure effects of its land-value model; the authors characterise that model as structurally favouring multi-family housing.[n] Tenant incidence is taken from Löffler & Siegloch rather than tested." Source row: Müller, R. & Wrede, M. (2026), CESifo Working Paper 13067, doi.org/10.65864/4vgkrlimtj; PDF www.ifo.de/DocDL/cesifo1_wp13067.pdf; Table 2 col. 2, fn. 10 (B-claim; working paper, not peer-reviewed). Also add to registry.csv (Title+Author+Year+URL; Wiki Page = places/germany).

Suggested content: German municipalities run by homeowner-oriented parties raised property-tax multipliers more where the state's valuation design gave tenants a higher per-m2 base (Müller & Wrede 2026, Table 2), with the effect tracking council party orientation rather than the homeownership share (Table 5) — a recent German instance of owner-aligned local governments exploiting a perceived tenant-borne burden. existing_wiki_coverage: places/germany.md (grundsteuer/BW section): covers the 2018 BVerfG ruling, the Öffnungsklausel, BW's modified land-value model (area x Bodenrichtwert; Steuermesszahl 1.3 per mille, 0.91 per mille for residential), Bavaria's Flächenmodell, the Löhr coalition, the BFH ruling of 20 May 2026 and the announced Verfassungsbeschwerde. It states 'The reform is too recent to have produced peer-reviewed incidence or behavioural evidence' and does not mention the federal model's rent-based valuation (standardized net rents), the state-by-state difference in rental vs owner-occupied bases, or the 2023-24 pre-reform surge in Hebesätze. research/loffler-siegloch-german-pass-through.md: the Hebesatz mechanism and pass-through (83% per ECONtribute DP 331; 'fully passed on ... after three years' per IZA DP 14195); explicitly cautions that Grundsteuer B is a land-plus-structure base. That page does not mention Müller & Wrede; the new paper relies on it for incidence, so a one-line back-reference is useful. research/buettner-german-land-tax-capitalization.md: Buettner (2003), 675 BW municipalities, Hebesatz variation and capitalization (elasticity about -0.31); no political-economy content. research/kolbe-berlin-land-value-appraisal.md: assessability (0.845 correlation); not bearing on this paper beyond the shared Grundsteuer-reform backdrop. objections/homevoters-will-block-lvt.md: Fischel's homevoter hypothesis, Prop 13, Cabral-Hoxby salience; no German evidence. research/murphy-seegert-implicit-land-taxes.md exists (cited by the paper). Zero hits in the digest for Müller or Wrede.
uncertainties: Scanner premise wrong: authors are not 'Ramona Müller (ifo) and Matthias Wrede (TU Darmstadt)'. The PDF's affiliations footnote gives Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg for both (Wrede also CESifo Research Network Fellow).

Scanner premise imprecise: 'states picked valuation models; some set higher tax bases for rentals'. The rental premium comes from the federal default model itself (treated: NRW, Rhineland-Palatinate, Saarland); the state-designed alternative models (BW, Bavaria, Hesse, Lower Saxony) are the control group. Hamburg is excluded from the sample (own model, endogeneity concern), as are Bremen and Schleswig-Holstein.

Scanner premise overstated: 'raised multipliers 15pp more where tenants bear the cost'. The estimate is a triple-difference relative to tenant-oriented councils and to opt-out states; 'tenants bear the cost' is an assumption (legal pass-through plus Löffler & Siegloch), not a finding. Baseline 15.017 is the conservative specification; the no-state-by-year-FE specification is 28.049; state-level bootstrap leaves p = 0.071.
The 3.6-year average post-announcement window is stated only in the abstract; not reproducible from the body text.

'Homeowner-friendly' is a classification of parties by manifesto keyword search plus an AI-based classification of small parties and a default coding of local lists as owner-friendly (Table A4); 92.92% of classifiable municipalities show no change in orientation over time. Sample drops 3,445 unclassifiable (smaller, higher-ownership, lower-multiplier) municipalities (Table A5).
Interpretation (anticipation before the revenue-neutral 2025 reform; avoiding media scrutiny) is the authors' reading; no direct evidence on council motives.
Page numbers above are from the text extraction's page markers and may be off by one; table and section labels are reliable.
Inference: treatment varies at state level across only seven states; the authors cluster by municipality and acknowledge the small-cluster problem (state-level bootstrap p = 0.071).

title: Fooks, Mullan, Mills, Yates & Willmott, "Elite welfare and the good fortune of just being there", Journal of Social Policy (CUP, online 12 October 2026)
what_was_fetched: Open access confirmed: the Cambridge Core page carries the statement 'This is an Open Access article, distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution licence (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)'. Fetched the full 19-page article PDF from Cambridge Core (dl2/elite-welfare.pdf, 453 kB; text extracted with pdftotext to item2-elite-welfare-fulltext.txt), the Cambridge Core landing page (saved as item2-cambridge-core-landing.txt, raw HTML in dl2/cambridge-landing.html), and the supplementary file S004727942610169Xsup001.docx (dl2/supp.docx; tables extracted to item2-supplementary-tables.txt) which holds the regression tables S.3-S.6 behind the paper's Figure 2.
verdict: REJECT as a wiki page or enrichment. The paper's empirical result is a DiD on executive pay after furlough receipt; its 'rent' is a loose political-economy usage (mixture of public-choice rent-seeking and Christophers' heterodox 'asset rent'), not economic rent in the wiki's Ricardian/Georgist sense. At most a one-clause mention could be justified in concepts/rent-seeking.md as an illustration of 'policy-enabled rent' claims, but nothing here bears on land, resource, or location rent or on any capture instrument, and the paper's step from a pay differential to 'unambiguous extraction of rent' is exactly the 'is it a rent?' flattening EDITORIAL 0 warns against. Recommend no action.
claim_grade: B for the empirical DiD (B-type claim; peer-reviewed article in Journal of Social Policy, CUP; recognised academic authors; EDITORIAL 4c Tier 1). D for the interpretive layer ('elite welfare', 'unambiguous extraction of rent'): D-type claim by the authors, not an empirical finding, and the DiD design does not identify rent (see uncertainties).

content_summary.design: Sample (p. 3): FTSE 350 as of 31 Dec 2021 with consistent executive-pay disclosure from March 2019, n = 246 (104 excluded, mainly REITs and investment vehicles, firms without UK operations, firms with <250 employees). Treatment: furlough (CJRS) receipt, hand-collected from annual-report notes and subsidiary accounts at Companies House; 91 of 246 (37%) received support in 2020, of which 56 (22.8%) in 2020 only and 35 (14.2%) in 2020 and 2021 (Table 1, p. 6). Generalised DiD (Wing et al. 2018) with two treatment groups; pre-period 1 April 2019 - 31 March 2020; post-periods 2021-22 and 2022-23 (2020-21 is the shock year); outcomes log(1 + pay) for CEO and CFO total pay and components; controls: employees, log sales, return on assets, leverage, executive-role change. Analysis samples: 227 CEO / 216 CFO firms (first set), 207 / 198 (second set). Parallel pre-trends reported in supplementary Figures S.2-S.3, Tables S.1-S.2. Funded by the Joseph Rowntree Charitable Trust (grant 3928); no competing interests.
content_summary.headline_wording: Abstract: "receipt of furlough support in 2020 was associated with significant increases in chief executive officer (CEO) performance pay and total remuneration in the immediate post-pandemic year." Results text (p. 8-9): for CEOs in firms supported in 2020 only, 'a positive significant difference-in-difference effect in the model for total remuneration' and 'a significant positive effect for performance-related pay'; no significant effects for basic salary, pension or benefits; 'For CEOs in firms receiving furlough support in 2020 and 2021, there were no significant effects on any component'; no CFO effects for the 2020-only group; CFO basic salary significant only for the 2020-and-2021 group; second-period models (2022-23): 'no statistically significant effects ... effects were limited to the year immediately following'.
content_summary.effect_sizes_from_supplement: Table S.3 (CEOs, 2021-22 vs 2019-20, N = 454 observations; robust s.e. in brackets; coefficients on log(1 + pay)): Furlough 2020 only: total pay 0.113* (0.056); performance pay 0.148* (0.071); basic pay 0.001 (0.013); pension/benefits 0.003 (0.029). Furlough 2020 & 2021: total -0.109 (0.08); performance -0.1 (0.1). Table S.4 (CFOs): 2020 only total 0.027 (0.057), performance 0.039 (0.065); 2020 & 2021 basic pay 0.037* (0.017). Table S.5 (CEOs, 2022-23 vs 2019-20): 2020 only total -0.017 (0.067), performance 0.023 (0.089). Table S.6 (CFOs): 2020 only total -0.056 (0.059). Significance key: * p < .05, + p < .1. The main text and Figure 2 give no point estimates; the exact figures exist only in the supplement. Because outcomes are log(1+pay) with pay apparently in GBP million (Table 2 is in GBP m), the coefficients are not clean percentage effects; the paper does not translate them. Descriptives (Table 2, p. 7, GBP m): mean CEO total pay 2.95 (2019-20), 3.15 (2021-22), 3.45 (2022-23); performance pay 1.92, 2.16, 2.40. Fig. 1: CEO/CFO pay fell from 2.95/1.58 to 2.37/1.27 in 2020-21 and recovered to 3.15/1.76.
content_summary.definition_of_elite_welfare: Introduction p. 2 and Discussion p. 10: "We define elite welfare as elite income generated through activities, opportunities and relationships that are (1) largely free from competitive restraints and either unmoored from value-producing activities or derived from assets that are scarce or artificially made scarce, and (2) have been directly or indirectly facilitated by policy decision-making or public expenditure, whether by design, through tolerated omission, or as an unintended effect." Intent is declared irrelevant to the classification (p. 14).
content_summary.definition_of_rent_and_citations: Section 'Rent and elite welfare', pp. 11-12. Opens: 'A clear, settled and widely agreed-upon definition of rent has proved elusive (Stratford, 2023)', citing Piketty ('any undue or unjustified income') and listing rival senses (excess over opportunity cost, over competitive price, income from ownership/control of a resource; Sayer 2023, Stratford 2023). Stratford is cited only for that proposition; the paper does not adopt, test or engage Stratford's taxonomy. It adopts Christophers (2019, 'The problem of rent', Critical Historical Studies) two-way split: (a) 'orthodox rents' = unearned income from unproductive activity redistributing rather than creating wealth, via public policy under limited competition (rent-seeking: tariffs, quotas, procurement padding, political cronyism, tax avoidance, below-market asset transfers; Congleton et al. 2008; Krueger 2008; Lambsdorff 2002; Kaufmann & Siegelbaum 1997); (b) 'heterodox rents' = returns from monopoly control of assets 'that are scarce or artificially made scarce' (Christophers 2019, 2020 Rentier Capitalism; Sayer 2023), with assets including infrastructure, patents and outsourcing contracts 'and assets that simply exist, such as land'. Also cites Mazzucato & Rodrik (2024, industrial policy with conditionalities) for the 'threshold of rent extraction' in subsidies, not Mazzucato's rent writings; Christophers 2023 (rentierization of the UK economy), Piketty 2014, Stiglitz 2015a-c, Eggertsson et al. 2021. On executive pay as rent: Bebchuk et al. 2002, Bivens & Mishel 2013, Edmans et al. 2017 (noted as sceptical about quantifying the rent share of pay). Operational test for 'rent extraction' in subsidies (p. 12): support 'confers an economic advantage on terms unavailable in the market, is weakly conditional, and gains ... are retained by owners, executives or other elite actors without commensurate public return'. Discussion claims the DiD finding 'reveals an unambiguous extraction of rent' (p. 9) while conceding 'Our design, of course, does not directly observe the board-level mechanisms behind the differential' (p. 10).
content_summary.land_content: Land appears only as one example of a 'heterodox' rent asset (Christophers 2020) and in the Teesworks case (p. 15: Redcar steelworks site; developers' option to buy the land cut from market value to a fixed GBP 1 per acre; public liabilities of GBP 560 million vs GBP 45 million in dividends, citing the Ridgwell et al. 2024 independent review). No mention of Ricardo, George, land value tax, or capture instruments.

existing_wiki_coverage: concepts/economic-rent.md defines rent as 'the payment to any factor of production in excess of what is required to bring it into — or keep it in — its current use' and builds from Smith, Ricardo and George; concepts/rent-seeking.md covers public-choice rent-seeking, Tullock/Krueger, Khan-style 'not all rents are alike', and subsidy rent-seeking cases; narratives/the-rentier-economy.md frames rentier capitalism as 'a rising share of income rewards asset ownership and economic rent — above all land under housing'; research/christophers-rentier-capitalism.md covers Christophers; research/mazzucato-mapping-rents.md and research/mazzucato-value-of-everything.md exist. Zero wiki hits for Stratford (2023), 'elite welfare', furlough, executive pay as rent, Fooks, Mullan, Tom Mills, Willmott. The paper's second half re-describes ground the wiki already covers (Christophers' orthodox/heterodox split, rent-seeking), so nothing new would be added on the concept side.
scanner_flags: Scanner: 'furlough receipt in 2020 raised CEO performance pay post-pandemic'. The paper says 'associated with' (DiD, no causal language in the abstract), and the effect is confined to firms supported in 2020 only (56 of 246 firms); the 35 firms supported in both 2020 and 2021 show no significant effect, CFOs show no total-pay effect, and no effect remains in 2022-23.

Scanner: 'frames elite rent extraction via public policy as a parallel welfare system' is accurate. 'Serves rentier-capitalism / economic-rent content' overstates the fit: the paper's rent is not the wiki's economic rent.
Scanner: 'Cites Stratford' is true but incidental (one citation to say definitions are contested).
uncertainties: Judgment on 'rent': The paper's own operational criterion for rent extraction is a pay differential after weakly conditioned subsidy, with no test of whether the differential exceeds a reservation wage, opportunity cost or competitive price; it acknowledges alternative explanations (remuneration committees rewarding CEOs for steering firms through the crisis, p. 10). That is a looser political-economy usage (policy-facilitated windfall), partly overlapping public-choice rent-seeking and partly Christophers' monopoly-asset sense, not Ricardian or Georgist economic rent (surplus over the supply price of a fixed or privileged factor).

The Table S.3-S.6 row labels read 'Furlough: 2020 only' and 'Furlough: 2020 & 2021'; the supplement does not label them as period x treatment interactions, although with firm fixed effects they must be the DiD terms. The mapping to the paper's Figure 2 coefficients was inferred, not stated.
Corporate results are from a single post-period (2021-22) and a small treated group; the authors say sector analysis is infeasible.

If editors still want a mention, the only defensible home is a one-clause example under concepts/rent-seeking.md with the explicit caveat that the pay differential is not shown to be rent; a Tier 1 peer-reviewed source, but low marginal value. No anchor sentence is given because the verdict is REJECT.

verdict: REJECT the history page as a source or enrichment (advocacy narrative, EDITORIAL 4c Tier 2/3, no independent coverage, several claims that conflict with or go beyond the wiki; the party's own officer page is placeholder text). DEFER any organizations/ page: the Electoral Commission register has NO registration under the name 'Georgist Party of Britain' or any 'Georgist' description; the only registered entity the site's own narrative points to is PP1912 'Shared Ground' (formerly Young People's Party). Revisit if (a) the register shows the Georgist name or a Georgist description for PP1912 or a new registration, or (b) independent news coverage appears. If the editors nonetheless want a stub now, the only Tier 1 anchor available is the EC record for PP1912 (facts below), written as 'Shared Ground (UK political party)' with the Georgist-successor claim attributed to the party's own site.
claim_grade: D for the history narrative as an evidentiary source (A-type historical claims with no citations; advocacy body, Tier 2/3 under 4c: usable only for the party's own account of itself). The EC register record is A-type, Tier 1 (official body), but it does not support the specific claim that a body called the Georgist Party of Britain is registered.

content_summary.page_content: History page (12.6k chars; H1 'Six centuries of the same argument'): 1381 and Tudor anti-enclosure revolts; Levellers and Winstanley's Diggers (St George's Hill 1649, 'common treasury'); Physiocrats Quesnay, Turgot, Mirabeau and 'Turgot's impôt unique'; Paine's Agrarian Justice (1797) and Thomas Spence; Smith, Ricardo, J.S. Mill and the Land Tenure Reform Association; Henry George and Progress and Poverty (1879), lecture tours of 1882 and 1884, Scottish and English Land Restoration Leagues; the 1909 People's Budget and Churchill; Snowden 1931; overseas application (Australia, NZ, South Africa, western Canada, Denmark's Retsforbundet, Pittsburgh and Scranton); a 'decisive century' section on Taiwan, South Korea, Japan, Singapore, Hong Kong, mainland China and the Gulf states; a quotation gallery (George, Smith, Paine, Mill, Lloyd George, Churchill, Tolstoy, Twain, Sun Yat-sen, Einstein) and a list of 'many more' (Marshall, Sun Yun-suan, Friedman, Stiglitz, Krugman, Vickrey, Tobin, Simon, FDR, Attlee, Keir Hardie, Shaw, Keller, Dewey, Huxley, Magie). No citations, footnotes or dates of authorship. Home page: platform of a 5% annual land charge and a flat 20% income tax; 'Britain's land alone is worth some GBP 8.5 trillion'; 'GBP 360bn the rent Britain's land yields every year'; membership GBP 20 a year; a 'Land in the news' strip linking Neidle/Tax Policy Associates (July 2026), a Commons committee (Oct 2025) and The Guardian (Aug 2026).
content_summary.party_self_description: About page: the party 'now campaigns under its present name' and is 'the continuation of the party Mark Wadsworth helped found. Registered with the Electoral Commission'; founded April 2012 'as the Young People's Party', registered with the EC under that name, stood in the 2015 and 2017 general elections (Folkestone & Hythe, Epping Forest, Cities of London & Westminster, City of Durham); later renamed Shared Ground 'after the Electoral Commission refused its first choice, Common Ground'. Strategy statement: 'We want Georgists in power ... We will not pretend it has to be this party's MPs who do it.'
content_summary.electoral_commission_record: Register queried 2026-11-02 (JSON API, entity types political party + minor party, GB/NI/none, statuses registered and deregistered): queries 'georgist', 'georgism', 'Georgist Party of Britain', 'single tax' return 0 results; 'Wadsworth' returns 0. Control: query 'Labour Party' returns 7 results and the PP53 record shows Andrew Burnham as Leader, so the search was working. Query 'Young People's Party' returns exactly one entity: PP1912 'Shared Ground'. Record PP1912: status Registered; register Great Britain; date registered 5 June 2012; Date last party-name change authorised 31 October 2025; party description 'Shared Ground formerly Young People's Party' (first approved 19 August 2021); one emblem first approved 6 April 2016; officers Mr Thomas Hall (Leader and Nominating Officer), Mr Sean Lee Rice (Treasurer); address Wren House, Garden Cl, Newbury, Berkshire RG14 6PR; fielding candidates in England, Scotland and Wales; exempt from quarterly donation and transaction returns; no company registration number. None of these officers or this address appears on the party website. A UK party may contest elections only under its registered name or an approved description, so the absence of any Georgist name or description means the site's 'Registered with the Electoral Commission' line, read as registration of 'The Georgist Party of Britain', is not borne out by the register. The register does not itself assert that PP1912 and georgistparty.uk are the same organisation; that link rests on the party's own narrative plus the 'formerly Young People's Party' description.
content_summary.companies_house: Name searches for 'georgist' and 'shared ground' on Companies House return no entity with a Georgist name; the 'Shared Ground' hits (e.g. Shared Ground Ltd, Bath, incorporated 8 March 2026; Shared Ground Foundation, Nottingham, 2015) are unrelated by address and nothing links them to PP1912. The site cites no company. No Companies House anchor exists.
content_summary.independent_corroboration: Wikipedia's constituency article for Cities of London and Westminster lists 'Young People's Party UK' candidate Benjamin Weenen (43 votes, 0.1%) at the General Election 2017, corroborating one of the four named candidacies; the other three constituencies' Wikipedia articles did not mention the party (Wikipedia is navigation-grade, not evidence). The claim that Mark Wadsworth was a founder and officer, and his death in March 2023, were not independently verified; the EC register lists neither as an officer (Wadsworth returns 0 results). Do not repeat the personal claims about him in the wiki without a reliable source.

Scanner: 'verify Electoral Commission registration before citing the party legal status' - done: no register entry under the Georgist name; see above. The scanner's 'registered-details line' is therefore unreliable as a legal-status source.

Scanner analogue wrong: organizations/commonwealth-land-party is the US Single Tax Party (renamed 1924), not a UK precedent. The relevant UK pages are organizations/labour-land-campaign (founded 1983), organizations/henry-george-foundation-uk (established January 1929), organizations/land-tenure-reform-association (1869), events/1909-peoples-budget, people/philip-snowden.

Scanner: 'Land Restoration League pages in the digest' - none exist. The only wiki mentions of the Scottish Land Restoration League are in texts/thy-kingdom-come.md and the public-domain Life of Henry George transcription; there is no page on either League.
existing_wiki_coverage: organizations/commonwealth-land-party (US, stub, 1924 rename of the Single Tax Party; Wikipedia-sourced). organizations/henry-george-foundation-uk: 'was established in January 1929 to administer a Trust Fund' (HGF's own About page). organizations/labour-land-campaign: founded 1983, campaigns within the Labour movement for land rent collection. organizations/land-tenure-reform-association: founded 1869 at Mill's initiative; programme 1871. events/1909-peoples-budget: four land duties enacted in the Finance (1909-10) Act 1910 at modest rates; repealed 1920 (Chamberlain, Hansard 19 April 1920; Finance Act 1920 s.57). people/philip-snowden: Finance Act 1931 land value tax, 'suspended in 1932 and repealed before it ever took effect' (Hansard 5 June 1934). people/winston-churchill and texts/churchill-mother-of-monopolies-1909: the Edinburgh speech of 17 July 1909. places/taiwan and concepts/land-value-increment-tax: LVIT regular progressive rates of 20%, 30%, 40%. places/singapore: state owns about 90% of land 'up from 44% in 1960'. places/denmark: 1957-60 Justice Party coalition. people/andy-burnham exists. No wiki page on the Georgist Party of Britain, Shared Ground, or the Young People's Party.
claims_contradicting_or_unsupported: Henry George Foundation dated 'from 1907' (Application overseas section: 'the Henry George Foundation from 1907'). The wiki (HGF's own statement) gives January 1929; the party's own About page says 'The Henry George Foundation, founded in 1929' and attributes 1907 to the United Committee for the Taxation of Land Values. Internal contradiction plus conflict with wiki.

Snowden: 'A second attempt in Snowden's 1931 budget died with the government that passed it.' The wiki records the 1931 land value tax as suspended in 1932 and repealed in 1934 (Hansard 5 June 1934), i.e. it outlived the Labour government by about three years. Loose or inaccurate.

Churchill: placed 'in Parliament' and quoted as 'contributes nothing to the process from which his own enrichment is derived'. The wiki locates the passage in the Edinburgh speech of 17 July 1909 (King's Theatre), not the Commons; the wording appears in the wiki's text of that speech ('he contributes nothing even to the process from which his own enrichment is derived'). Venue wrong, quotation abridged.

Taiwan: 'taxed land value increments at up to 50 per cent'. The wiki, citing current law (Land Tax Act Art. 33), gives progressive rates of 20/30/40%; no 50% figure appears. Unsupported unless a historical rate schedule is cited.
Singapore: public ownership 'rose from roughly a third of the island to about nine-tenths'. The wiki says 44% in 1960 to about 90%; a baseline of one-third is unsourced.

Hong Kong ('a third or more of public spending') and mainland China ('exceeded a third of total government income') revenue shares: no citation on the page; no matching figure located in the wiki's Hong Kong page.

Physiocrats: 'Turgot's impôt unique is the ancestor of every single-tax proposal'. The impôt unique is usually credited to Quesnay and the Marquis de Mirabeau; the wiki's Turgot page does not describe Turgot as its author. Unsupported attribution.

'Progress and Poverty ... outsold in the English-speaking world only by the Bible': a widely repeated claim; the wiki says only 'one of the bestselling books of the 19th century'. Unsupported by any citation.

Mark Twain quotation about 'a hundred vacant lots': no source given and no wiki support; treat as unverified attribution. The Mill quotation ('Landlords grow richer in their sleep ...') is a paraphrase of Principles of Political Economy; the page states quotations are 'abridged'.

Sympathizer lists (Attlee, Keir Hardie, FDR, Krugman, Huxley, Dewey, Keller, Shaw; 'Stiglitz showed that a well-run city could fund itself from land rent alone'): no citations; some are contested characterizations (Henry George theorem conditions).
Quantities on the home page ('GBP 8.5 trillion', 'GBP 360bn a year') are unsourced party statements.

'Georgism shaped the early Labour movement, Liberal land reform and the Irish land agitation alike' and 'common property of the British left and the radical right': interpretive claims without sources.
uncertainties: The EC API 'Date last change to primary name authorised' of 31 October 2025 conflicts with the About page's account that the Shared Ground name predates March 2023; the description 'Shared Ground formerly Young People's Party' was first approved 19 August 2021. The register does not reveal the prior primary name history, so the exact date PP1912 became 'Shared Ground' is unresolved.

Whether PP1912 'Shared Ground' is the same body as the people running georgistparty.uk is unconfirmed by any independent source; if the site's operators are a different group, 'Registered with the Electoral Commission' would be false for them.
No search of news archives beyond the EC register, Companies House and Wikipedia was done; the scanner reported no independent coverage and none was found here.
Notability under 4c: a registered micro-party with 43 votes at its one documented contest is unlikely to clear the bar for its own page without independent coverage.
